Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services. It reduces the amount of goods and services a unit of money can buy.

A price increase in one item, neighborhood, or asset class is not by itself inflation. Economists measure broad price changes with indexes such as the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index and the Consumer Price Index.

Prices can rise when demand grows faster than the economy's ability to supply goods and services, when production costs rise, or when expectations and contracts carry price increases forward. The mix differs across episodes.
Monetary policy can influence aggregate demand and inflation expectations, but it does not directly set the price of each item or local market.
Local price shocks and the AI boom

A concentration of high-paid workers or newly liquid equity can increase competition for scarce housing in one region. That can raise local home prices and possibly rents; it does not establish a broad rise in the price level across the economy.
Local price shocks and the AI boom

The Federal Reserve defines inflation as a general increase in prices across the economy. A local housing or restaurant price change is evidence about that market, not enough to establish local or national inflation by itself.

Inflation is a rising general price level; deflation is a falling general price level. The trade-off is not a choice between two equally desirable targets: rapid or unpredictable movement in either direction can disrupt decisions, while persistent deflation can worsen downturns and make debts harder to repay.

Modern central banks generally aim for low, stable inflation rather than a perfectly constant price level. That leaves room for relative prices to adjust while reducing the risks associated with high inflation and deflation.

Lower prices for a particular service are not deflation unless the overall price level is falling. Higher home values are asset-price inflation in ordinary speech, but they are not the same measure as consumer-price inflation.
Federal Reserve: Historical approaches to monetary policy describes the costs of unstable inflation and deflation, including harder debt repayment when prices fall unexpectedly.
St. Louis Fed: Inflation, disinflation, and deflation distinguishes inflation from disinflation and deflation.
In this trade-off, deflation means a broad and sustained fall in prices, not simply slower inflation or one item becoming cheaper.

Falling prices can benefit buyers in the short run, but expected deflation can lead households and firms to delay spending. It also raises the real burden of debts fixed in money terms and can leave central banks with less room to reduce interest rates.

In this trade-off, inflation means a broad rise in prices over time. Mild, stable inflation gives households and businesses a predictable planning environment and lets relative prices adjust without requiring nominal prices and wages to fall.
When inflation is high or unpredictable, purchasing power shifts between borrowers and savers, contracts become harder to plan around, and people spend effort adjusting prices rather than producing.

It uses Anthropic's open-source sandbox runtime: Seatbelt (sandbox-exec) on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux. Writes are limited to the working directory, and network traffic goes through an allowlisting proxy.
Anthropic reports about 84% fewer permission prompts with it on. Apple marks sandbox-exec as deprecated, which leaves its future uncertain.
It's enough for iterative pair programming.

Docker/Sandboxes: a microVM per sandbox, each with its own kernel and Docker daemon. The workspace syncs both ways, network goes through a proxy with domain allow and deny lists, and Claude runs with --dangerously-skip-permissions. In February 2026 this needed Docker Desktop 4.58+, which is free only for organizations with fewer than 250 employees and under $10M in revenue. Its downsides were growing disk use and some effort to manage credentials.

Mostly in what you share into the sandbox. Read access matters more than write access: if the agent can read ~/.ssh and reach the network, your keys are gone.
Network access is the second risk. Docker Sandboxes filters by domain and Tart filters packets. With Lima and OrbStack you configure iptables yourself.
He gives CVE-2025-9074 as an example. It exposed Docker Desktop's Engine API to containers without authentication.
The VM boundary is the security boundary. Containers, devcontainers and Seatbelt profiles add defense in depth but are not a different tier.
Use /sandbox for a pair programmer. Use a VM for agents that need Docker, MCP and network access.

The Ondes Martenot is an early electronic musical instrument invented in 1928 by French cellist and radio engineer Maurice Martenot. Known for its ethereal, voice-like timbre, it became a favorite among avant-garde composers and remains one of the most expressive electronic instruments of the 20th century.
Play method: Keyboard and ring-controlled pitch ribbon
Notable composers: Olivier Messiaen, André Jolivet, Jonny Greenwood
The Interim Computer Museum (ICM) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that preserves and shares the history of computing through hands-on exhibits using vintage hardware with modern enhancements.
ICM operates in partnership with SDF Public Access UNIX System, Inc., a 501(c)(7) membership organization. Membership supports community events, remote access, and artifact preservation.
The museum is open by appointment to supporters Saturday through Monday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
The museum is at SDF.ORG, 952 Industry Dr., , WA 98188, south of Seattle and about 10 minutes from (SEATAC).

Interim Computer Museum describes MIT-MC, a DECSYSTEM-10 KL10 Model 1080 operated by the MIT MACSYMA Consortium, as a major ARPANET node and an influential environment for symbolic computing and artificial intelligence.
MIT-MC ran the Incompatible Timesharing System (ITS), hosted MACSYMA, and connected programmers, researchers, and students through remote access.
The preservation story connects with the book discussion through MIT Project MAC, the MIT AI Lab, and the article's account of the MIT hacker ethic.

Adversarial interoperability is a term Person/Cory Doctorow helped popularize in a 2019 series of Electronic Frontier Foundation Deeplinks essays (often under his EFF byline): it names compatibility achieved without an incumbent platform or product maker’s permission—often over their active opposition—and treats that practice as structurally important for competition and user agency.

Against plain interoperability. In the October 2019 roundup, interoperability is “the act of making a new product or service work with an existing product or service,” while adversarial interoperability is when you “create a new product or service that plugs into the existing ones without the permission of the companies that make them.” Doctorow illustrates that contrast with third-party printer ink, alternative app stores, and independent repair shops using compatible parts.

Against cooperative interoperability. In the July 2019 taxonomy, “cooperative interoperability” covers standards and interfaces vendors want others to use; by contrast, adversarial interoperability is when “an add-on comes along that connects to a product whose manufacturer is outright hostile to it.” The piece defines it explicitly: “When a manufacturer builds a new product that plugs into an existing one despite the latter’s manufacturer’s hostility, that’s called ‘adversarial interoperability’.” Examples given there include third-party inkjet ink, unauthorized iPhone apps, homebrew console games, and DVRs that record cable content on the user’s terms.

Wrested compatibility, not a handshake. In the June 2019 historical essay, Doctorow distinguishes a merely interoperable product from an adversarially interoperable one: Apple’s iWork succeeded because Pages, Numbers, and Keynote could exchange files with Microsoft Office through “diligent reverse-engineering and reimplementation,” with compatibility “wrested from the incumbent” and kept current despite Microsoft’s updates—not because Microsoft cooperated.

Dominance as liability. The same essay gives Doctorow’s macro-level slogan: “Adversarial interoperability converts market dominance from an unassailable asset to a liability.” The mechanism is that a rival can turn the incumbent’s installed base into a reachable audience (his example arc: Facebook interoperating with MySpace users so messages back to MySpace advertised Facebook).

Ongoing access vs one-off export. Doctorow argues adversarial interoperability goes beyond typical “data portability” (bulk export once): users need “the ability to have ongoing access to a service that you’re in the process of migrating away from,” not only a snapshot export.

Users’ counteroffer. He frames tools like ad blockers and independent repair as users exercising adversarial interoperability as a “bargaining chip” in coercive take-it-or-leave-it “negotiations” over surveillance and lock-in—making a market where rival firms cannot yet discipline the platform.

Doctorow groups interoperability into indifferent (the vendor does not care), cooperative (the vendor welcomes or standardizes attachment), and adversarial (the vendor opposes attachment but third parties plug in anyway). The October hub colloquially glosses that ladder as moving from “I don’t care if you plug your thing into my product” to “please plug your thing” to “dang it, stop plugging your thing into my product!” with pointers back to the July taxonomy piece.
Legal and technical friction (as Doctorow narrates it)

The same EFF series ties the decline of routine adversarial interoperability to a “thicket” of law and policy—Doctorow and EFF point to the CFAA, DMCA §1201, software patents, DRM, and contract terms—as tools incumbents use after “climbing the adversarial ladder” to “pull it up behind them.”
